items.gist: The rite visualizes and transfers a blazing mantra into the disciple through nyāsa, leading toward the supreme principle.
The text distinguishes nāda-vedha from bindu-vedha, locating the mind at the bindu and awakening the goal through it.
Śākta vedha is performed through śakti-utterance and scent, piercing the whole world by the bhramara method.
The supreme śakti rises from the birthplace adorned with five phaṇas, enters Brahma's place, and pierces the body as bhujaṅga vedha.
When mind is exhausted, parānanda arises; paravedha is beyond senses, mind, and all bhāvas.
Some teachers divide the ninefold piṇḍa; another method uses a triangular maṇḍala and mantra to pierce knots.
Consciousness is gathered and whirled through the nāḍīs, then placed in a cakra, producing immediate realization.
A bright śikhā purifies the body and, through meditation on one's own maṇḍala, reflects the worlds.
A beautiful form arising from the brow-bindu is meditated upon and made one's own, yielding union.
The eightfold vijñāna is moved through the nāḍīs, strengthening identification and producing divine knowledge in the heart-space.
The subtle and gross piṇḍas are distinguished and progressively pacified, leading to the supreme state.
Each bodily cakra is illumined in sequence, and sthāna vedha grants its corresponding fruit.
The three principal nāḍīs and their unification produce varied nāḍī vedha and attainment of awakening.
A great yogī forcibly bursts another nāḍī and casts even a siddha down to earth.
The guru makes the disciple Śiva by contemplating non-duality across all cakras, without being stained.
The disciple enters before the guru; through mutual gazing and sameness, both attain the unmanas state and become one with Śiva.
Gods seek liberation; when the rite swallows the ray-wheel, it is called Śārvī dīkṣā, giving motionless liberation.
External breath and darkness are withdrawn, then the five knots are pierced by saṃghaṭṭa, granting Śiva-nature to all beings.
After initiation, a caru is cooked and eaten with sādhakas, destroying great sins.
The next day a yāga is performed; whatever pleases the guru is offered, and cakracaryā is called saṃcāra.
The disciple drinks the filled vessel only by guru's command, after worship and offerings, and never otherwise.
One should not act with those ruled by greed and delusion; the disciple performs this rite at the beginning, middle, and end of yāga.
The secret procedure has been thoroughly discussed from the guru's experienced teaching.
